User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes

Jonathan Kozaczuk    Zheng Dong    Noyan Evirgen    Keivan Majidi    Eddie K. H. Ng Affiliation: Chris Porter   Qi Zhao   Jia Geng   Changmao Li   Brandon R. Feng Affiliation: Amazon
Abstract

User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.

1 Introduction

Modern personalization, recommendation, and user-modeling systems aim to understand users and tailor experiences to their preferences. Doing so often relies on representing users in the form of user embeddings: dense vectors representing their historical actions and preferences that can be used as input into collaborative filtering or deep learning (DL) models (Raza et al., 2025; Ning et al., 2024). These embeddings can be generated in a variety of ways, from classical count matrices to transformer-based sequence encoders (Wang et al., 2025).

Although user embeddings can encode rich patterns of user behavior, they are not inherently interpretable. This has several important implications. For example, it is not straightforward to identify why a specific recommendation is made for a particular user, or audit what information an embedding contains about a user. It is also not typically possible to query the embedding space using natural language as in text-based semantic search. In this work, we show that the superposition hypothesis from mechanistic interpretability (MI) provides a framework for understanding this opacity and recovering transparent behavioral structure.

A key result in MI is that transformer neurons encode human-interpretable concepts in superposition, recoverable by sparse dictionary methods such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and auto-interpretable from activating examples (Bricken et al., 2023; Cunningham et al., 2024). We argue and empirically demonstrate that user embeddings encode behavioral modes in the same way, making them a natural new test case for the MI framework beyond the transformer-residual-stream settings where it was developed. The resulting sparse decomposition yields an interpretable user representation without per-user labeling or text-based embeddings, enabling applications from user insights to natural language semantic search.

There are other natural approaches for assigning behavioral modes to users. One can define a taxonomy of modes a priori and classify each user into a combination, or prompt an LLM to label each user’s interaction history directly. Both approaches require access to raw interaction data and domain-specific configuration, neither operates in the embedding space, and per-user LLM labeling is prohibitively expensive at scale. Our post-hoc decomposition requires only pre-trained embeddings, discovers modes unsupervised from the data, and produces graded mode assignments (e.g., distinguishing a casual from a devoted dog owner) rather than binary labels. It also produces dictionary vectors that support downstream embedding-space operations such as retrieval and audience characterization. We validate this framework on synthetic data with known ground-truth modes, embedded both by mean-pooling and by a trained transformer encoder (mode recovery measured directly), and on two public datasets where zero-shot natural-language audience retrieval over the decomposition serves as an external interpretability test, demonstrating faithful recovery, more behaviorally distinct features than K-Means encoding, and retrieval matching or exceeding classical sparse and text-embedding baselines.

2 Related Work

Sparse autoencoders for embedding interpretability. SAEs were first applied to language model activations to extract monosemantic features from polysemantic neurons (Cunningham et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2023), and have since been scaled to large frontier models (Gao et al., 2024; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024). Recent work extends SAEs to text embedding spaces (Ye et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025) and to non-LLM embeddings in other domains including speaker, pathology, cell-image, radiology, and CLIP representations (Pluth et al., 2025; Le et al., 2024; Dasdelen et al., 2025; Abdulaal et al., 2024; Zaigrajew et al., 2025). These methods all ground latents in semantics available in the input modality (text tokens, images, audio frames). Our work extends SAE decomposition to behavioral embeddings that encode non-textual interaction sequences, requiring a different interpretation pipeline and enabling natural language semantic search over embedding spaces that were never trained on text.

SAEs for recommender systems. Two concurrent works apply SAEs in recommender settings. Spíšák et al. (2026) insert an SAE between the encoder and decoder of a collaborative filtering autoencoder, and Klenitskiy et al. (2025) apply SAEs to the hidden states of transformer-based sequential recommenders. Both target recommendation steering or control. Our work differs in that we decompose pre-trained user embeddings post-hoc without modifying the recommendation model, evaluate against known ground-truth behavioral modes, and validate interpretability of the decomposition directly on audience understanding and natural-language semantic search.

Criticism of SAEs and random baselines. Korznikov et al. (2026) show that SAEs with frozen-random decoders can match fully trained SAEs in high-dimensional LLM residual streams at high overcompleteness, and Cui et al. (2026) further demonstrates SAEs can fail to recover ground-truth LLM features. We directly address these concerns in Section 4 by comparing against the soft-frozen-decoder baseline of (Korznikov et al., 2026) on our synthetic setup, where the ground-truth modes allow a direct measurement of per-user mixture-weight recovery. This equivalence does not hold at moderate overcompleteness (Section 4).

User-representation decomposition and disentanglement. Prior work on interpreting user representations takes two approaches. End-to-end disentanglement, as in MacridVAE and DisenHAN (Ma et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2025), incorporates disentanglement objectives into the upstream recommender at training time. Post-hoc decomposition applies unsupervised dictionary learning to pre-trained representations. Classical post-hoc methods include NMF, PCA, Archetypal Analysis, and k-means for behavior segmentation (Drachen et al., 2013), and topic models (LDA and extensions) which treat interactions as words drawn from latent topics and produce interpretable topics (Mukherjee et al., 2017; Chaudhuri et al., 2021). We take the post-hoc approach. In contrast to topic models, which operate on raw interactions, our method decomposes pre-trained user embeddings directly, leveraging the richer behavioral signal they encode (e.g., co-viewing sequence, rating intensity, genre co-occurrence) beyond what simple interaction counts capture. Our contribution includes the MI-grounded framework for analyzing user embeddings as sparse superpositions of behavioral concepts, allowing us to recover and identify behavioral modes in natural language. This enables zero-shot natural-language audience retrieval from the recovered modes.

Audience retrieval. The standard approach to audience retrieval is lookalike modeling: given a seed set of example users, find similar users in an embedding space (Liu et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024). These methods require pre-defined example users (“seeds”) and provide no transparency into what behavioral patterns drive the retrieved audience. Our method queries over automatically interpreted sparse behavioral modes, requiring neither seed users nor text-aligned training data.

3 Superposition from a generative model of user behavior

In this section, we analyze a simple generative model for user behavior to motivate why and how superposition arises in user embeddings. The derivation is exact in expectation for embedding functions that average per-observation features, and serves as a plausibility argument for deep-learning encoders via the superposition hypothesis, which we test empirically for transformer encoders in Sections 4 and 5 below. Consider a user 𝒰\mathcal{U} interacting in a specific environment 𝒲\mathcal{W}, where each interaction produces an observation 𝐳=(z1,…,zN)\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}) comprising NN observable features. A given user’s behavior in 𝒲\mathcal{W} is summarized as a matrix H𝒰H_{\mathcal{U}}, where (H𝒰)i​j=zj​(𝒰,ti)(H_{\mathcal{U}})_{ij}=z_{j}(\mathcal{U};t_{i}), the observed feature value for 𝒰\mathcal{U} at interaction tit_{i}. Here tit_{i} labels a particular interaction of 𝒰\mathcal{U} with the environment. Note that H𝒰H_{\mathcal{U}} is implicitly time-dependent, since a user’s interactions with the environment are dynamic. We will suppress time dependence throughout this study for simplicity, but at any given snapshot our methodology will apply.

We assume there exist a discrete set of behavioral modes, {𝒫k∣k=1,…,K}\{\mathcal{P}_{k}\mid k=1,\ldots,K\}, which are interpretable user types with associated distributions pk​(𝐳)p_{k}(\mathbf{z}) that define the mode’s behavior patterns. Modes can be defined at arbitrary granularity: one can always merge two modes into one or split a mode into finer sub-modes. Examples of behavioral modes might be dog lovers on a shopping platform, binge-watchers on a streaming service, or commute-dominated mobility patterns in a ride-sharing app. We further assume each user’s behavior is governed by a sparse subset of modes, with user-specific non-negative weights 𝐰∈ℝ≥0K\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}_{\geq 0}, ‖𝐰‖0≪K\|\mathbf{w}\|_{0}\ll K, ∑kwk=1\sum_{k}w_{k}=1. Conditioned on 𝐰\mathbf{w}, each interaction for a user 𝒰\mathcal{U} is drawn independently from the mixture

p𝒰​(𝐳)=∑k=1Kwk​pk​(𝐳).p_{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\,p_{k}(\mathbf{z}). (1)

The weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} captures both which modes are active and their relative prevalence in the user’s behavior. Equation (1) is a mixed-membership model: each user belongs to multiple modes simultaneously, with each interaction generated by one mode. When the observations are discrete (e.g., individual product purchases treated as tokens), this reduces to the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) generative model (Blei et al., 2003), with behavioral modes playing the role of topics and products playing the role of words. Our formulation generalizes this to continuous and vector-valued observations, but inherits the same core structure: a population of users, a shared set of latent modes, and sparse per-user mixtures.

3.1 Superposition in embedding space

A user embedding 𝐮\mathbf{u} for user 𝒰\mathcal{U} is defined by 𝐮=F⁡(H𝒰)\mathbf{u}=F(H_{\mathcal{U}}), with F:ℝT𝒰×N→ℝmF:\mathbb{R}^{T_{\mathcal{U}}\times N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}, where T𝒰T_{\mathcal{U}} is the user’s number of interactions (variable across users), mm is the embedding dimension, and typically m≪Nm\ll N. Common examples of FF include classical embedding models (e.g., SVD on a counts matrix) or neural networks (e.g., behavioral sequence encoders).

A key consequence of the generative model in Eq. (1) is that when FF is a sample mean of per-observation features ff (as with mean-pooled product embeddings), the user embedding inherits a sparse superposition structure in expectation:

𝐮≈∑k=1Kwk​𝐝k,where𝐝k≡𝔼z∼pk​[f⁡(z)]\mathbf{u}\approx\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\,\mathbf{d}_{k},\qquad\text{where}\quad\mathbf{d}_{k}\equiv\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_{k}}[f(z)] (2)

is the expected embedding of observations drawn purely from mode kk and f:ℝN→ℝmf:\mathbb{R}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} maps individual observations to their embeddings. User embeddings are therefore sparse linear superpositions of mode centroids 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k}. Analogous expressions hold for linearly-transformed sample-mean pooling, F=A⋅1T𝒰∑if(𝐳i)F=A\cdot\frac{1}{T_{\mathcal{U}}}\sum_{i}f(\mathbf{z}_{i}) for a fixed matrix AA (e.g., a projection), with the centroids replaced by their images A​𝐝kA\mathbf{d}_{k}. These centroids need not be orthogonal: modes with overlapping observation distributions (e.g., “coffee connoisseur” and “home barista”) produce correlated directions, and when m<Km<K even unrelated modes must share them. Both effects place the centroids in superposition in the sense of (Elhage et al., 2022), motivating the use of overcomplete sparse dictionaries rather than orthogonal decompositions for recovery.

Embeddings from nonlinear deep-learning encoders admit a similar structure, which we illustrate via the transformer case. Under the superposition hypothesis (Elhage et al., 2022), each residual-stream position satisfies 𝐫ℓ≈∑jaj(ℓ)​𝐝j\mathbf{r}_{\ell}\approx\sum_{j}a_{j}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{d}_{j}. For a user embedding formed by any linear pooling of positions (mean-pool, sum-pool), linearity gives 𝐮≈∑ja~j​𝐝j\mathbf{u}\approx\sum_{j}\tilde{a}_{j}\mathbf{d}_{j} with a~j\tilde{a}_{j} the matching linear combination of {aj(ℓ)}ℓ\{a_{j}^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell}. A mode 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} induces a distribution over observations and hence over transformer features. If the expected activations decompose linearly in the mode mix 𝐰\mathbf{w}, the feature directions sum into a mode-level centroid 𝐝~k=∑j𝔼pk​[a~j]​𝐝j\tilde{\mathbf{d}}_{k}=\sum_{j}\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[\tilde{a}_{j}]\,\mathbf{d}_{j} replacing 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k} in Eq. (2), where the expectation is over histories with interactions drawn from pkp_{k}. An SAE applied to pooled embeddings therefore recovers mode-level structure rather than individual transformer features. For single-position readouts (last-token, [CLS]) the linear-pooling argument does not apply directly. We conjecture that behavioral-mode resolution emerges from training dynamics, since the objective depends on aggregate sequence structure rather than individual items, but leave verification to future work. Our experiments mean-pool across final-layer positions, so the analysis above applies directly. When attention contextualizes interactions so the linearity-in-𝐰\mathbf{w} assumption fails, SAE latents may correspond to finer or composite structure rather than aligning one-to-one with the ground-truth 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k}. Since modes admit arbitrary granularity (Section 3), the recovered latents remain behavioral modes, at a granularity shaped by the encoder rather than fixed by the generative model.

Under the flat generative model of Eq. (1) with sample-mean FF, each 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} contributes a single direction 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k}, so any further splitting of 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k} across multiple SAE latents is artifactual feature splitting (Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024; Chanin et al., 2024). At the single-example level the L1L_{1} penalty favors a single aligned atom, but over a population of users the penalty can prefer finer-grained atoms that each activate on a distinct subset of users, reducing the total L1L_{1} mass under overcompleteness. Split features can be identified by decoder-direction similarity or correlated activations across users and merged post-hoc, which we validate on synthetic data in Section 4. For nonlinear FF, the previous paragraph identified an additional source of finer-grained latents from attention-driven context-dependence, and merging absorbs only the artifactual-splitting component.

3.2 Recovery via sparse autoencoders

Equation (2) implies that recovering behavioral modes from a population of user embeddings is a sparse dictionary learning problem: given {𝐮i}i=1M\{\mathbf{u}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}, find a dictionary D∈ℝm×dhiddenD\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\text{hidden}}} and sparse non-negative codes {𝐰^i}\{\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}\} such that 𝐮i≈D​𝐰^i\mathbf{u}_{i}\approx D\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}. The SAE’s dictionary width dhiddend_{\text{hidden}} is typically larger than the embedding dimension mm to accommodate superposition, and need not equal the ground-truth mode count KK.

This problem has classical solutions in the discrete observation domain: LDA recovers topics from token counts via variational inference, and NMF recovers non-negative factors from count matrices. However, these methods require access to the raw interaction data and cannot leverage the semantic geometry captured by modern embedding models. We instead operate directly on embeddings using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse dictionary representation of the input with sparsity enforced by an L1L_{1} penalty on encoder activations. In particular, the “vanilla” ReLU SAE is defined on an input embedding 𝐮\mathbf{u} as

𝐮^=Wdec​ReLU⁡(Wenc​𝐮+𝐛).\hat{\mathbf{u}}=W_{\rm dec}\,\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{\rm enc}\,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{b}). (3)

In terms of Eq. (2), the jj-th SAE latent estimates a mode weight and its decoder column estimates the mode direction:

w^j≡ReLU(Wenc𝐮+𝐛)j,(𝐝^j)ℓ≡(Wdec)ℓ​j,j=1,…,dhidden.\displaystyle\hat{w}_{j}\equiv\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{\rm enc}\,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{b})_{j},\qquad(\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{j})_{\ell}\equiv(W_{\rm dec})_{\ell j},\quad j=1,\ldots,d_{\text{hidden}}. (4)

The SAE is trained to minimize ℒ⁡(𝐮)=‖𝐮^−𝐮‖22+λ​∑j=1dhiddenw^j\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u})=\|\hat{\mathbf{u}}-\mathbf{u}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\text{hidden}}}\hat{w}_{j}, where the sparsity term drops the absolute value since w^j≥0\hat{w}_{j}\geq 0 after the ReLU. The decoder columns are unit-normalized so that they constitute unit vectors in the original embedding space.

Typically in mechanistic interpretability work, the SAE is overcomplete, with the hidden dimension larger than the input dimension (dhidden>md_{\rm hidden}>m), so that superposition can be disentangled. For user embeddings, the number of behavioral modes KK may be less than the embedding dimension mm, however the individual 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k} are still typically in superposition and non-orthogonal. The relevant overcomplete regime in our case is therefore dhiddend_{\rm hidden} large enough that the SAE can dedicate features to each mode, or to each sub-mode in the case of nonlinear encoders where behavioral modes split into finer directions. Note that this is not possible with techniques such as PCA, whose components are orthogonal by construction. We compare SAEs against classical sparse dictionary baselines including sparsified versions of PCA, ICA, NMF, and K-Means encoding in our experiments below. Each baseline captures part of the mode structure assumed by Eq. (2) but lacks at least one key property: overcompleteness (PCA/ICA), the ability to handle signed input (NMF), or the freedom for dictionary directions to point beyond cluster centers (kk-means encoding).

Provided the SAE recovers the underlying behavioral modes, its latents should have interpretable descriptions recoverable from the data. We obtain these via auto-interpretation (Bricken et al., 2023; Cunningham et al., 2024): for each SAE latent we pass activating and non-activating user examples with their interaction histories to an LLM and prompt it to identify the dominant pattern in the positives. The output is a set of empirical latents {𝒫^k}\{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{k}\}, each comprising a name 𝒩^k\hat{\mathcal{N}}_{k}, description 𝒟^k\hat{\mathcal{D}}_{k}, and basis vector 𝐝^k\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{k} in the original embedding space. This enables decomposing audiences in terms of behavioral modes and natural-language semantic search by selecting codes with highest semantic overlap with a query and retrieving users with the highest activations on those codes. The same auto-interpretation step can be applied to the classical sparse baselines. Additionally, the LLM outputs a confidence score alongside each name. Because the name and description are grounded in the vocabulary shown to the LLM (e.g., item titles, categories), latents whose defining axis falls outside that vocabulary receive lower confidence. These are typically finer-grained features in the nonlinear-FF regime. We expect such latents to remain monosemantic and interpretable under a richer vocabulary, but we gate on confidence ≥0.6{\geq}0.6 at retrieval to keep named features within the vocabulary’s resolution.

4 Experiments on Synthetic Data

Assuming behavioral mode superposition in embedding space, to what extent can SAEs and other methods faithfully recover behavioral modes under controlled conditions where the ground truth is known? That the embedding of a sparse mixture is a sparse combination of mode centroids follows from Eq. (2). However, it is not guaranteed that these centroids can be recovered from the embeddings alone. To test this, we construct synthetic user embeddings with known mode mixtures, apply the SAE, and measure whether its latents correspond to the true modes (no auto-interpretation is needed, since the ground truth is known). This validates recovery under the framework’s assumptions. Whether user embeddings extracted from real-world datasets exhibit the assumed structure is tested in Section 5. Classical baselines (PCA, ICA, K-Means encoding, NMF) test whether the structural constraints identified in Section 3.2 (enforced orthogonality, non-negative input, cluster-centered directions) bottleneck mode recovery.

Setup.

We define K=75K{=}75 behavioral modes (e.g., “dog lover”, “new parent”), each with a description and example products. Each of 100,000 synthetic users is assigned 2 to 6 active modes, chosen in proportion to mode popularity, with log-normal mixture weights (e.g., 0.7×\times“dog lover” + 0.3×\times“new parent”). We prompt Claude Sonnet 4 to write a purchase history for each user (median 55 orders) whose interactions follow these weights, plus 5 to 20% off-mode noise (see Appendix A). We chose K=75K{=}75 so that the embedding dimensions swept below (m=16m=16 to 128128) bracket the mode count. Item popularity is heavy-tailed, with the top 1% of items carrying 51% of interactions. We embed each product with all-mpnet-base-v2 and mean-pool over the user’s interactions, yielding a 768-dimensional embedding that is a superposition of the underlying modes. To further vary the amount of superposition, we follow the techniques in (Bingham and Mannila, 2001) and project these embeddings onto random directions in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}. The dimension mm is varied across the experiment. Finally, the embeddings are standardized and L2L_{2}-normalized.

We train an SAE with dhidden=300d_{\rm hidden}=300 (4×4{\times} overcomplete relative to ground truth) with an adaptive sparsity penalty ensuring that the mean number of active latents (L0L_{0}) matches the ground-truth mean number of modes per user. We compare against six baselines: random projections onto 300 unit vectors with ReLU, sparsified versions of PCA and FastICA, K-Means encoding (cosine similarity to K-Means centroids passed through ReLU and thresholded to match the SAE’s L0L_{0}, following (Coates and Ng, 2012)), the soft-frozen decoder SAE of (Korznikov et al., 2026), and NMF on shifted (non-negative) embeddings. Matching the ground-truth mode count, K-Means encoding uses 75 components, and PCA, ICA, and NMF use min⁡(75,m)\min(75,m). NMF keeps its natural sparsity (no post-hoc thresholding). K-Means is additionally evaluated with 512 components to isolate raw capacity from decomposition quality. Further details are in Appendix A.

To measure ground truth recovery, each component is matched to its best ground-truth mode by Pearson correlation between component activations and mode weights across users. This mapping is many-to-one: when multiple components map to the same mode, their activations are summed. We also report SAE results after merging features whose decoder directions have cosine similarity > 0.45{>}\,0.45.

Results.

We evaluate three metrics (Fig. 1, all at matched L0L_{0}): per-feature correlation (Pearson rr between each component and its best-matching mode), code–GT alignment (per-user cosine similarity after mapping components to modes), and feature recovery (fraction of modes with a decoder direction at cosine ≥ 0.7{\geq}\,0.7). An oracle ceiling (least-squares from projected embeddings to ground-truth weights) bounds what any linear method can achieve at each mm.

In the high-superposition regime m<K=75m<K=75, the SAE matches or exceeds every classical baseline in Fig. 1 on mode recovery and stays close to the oracle ceiling on code–GT alignment. K-Means encoding holds steady near 80%80\% recovery (tied with the SAE at m=16m=16) and matches or slightly exceeds the SAE on alignment at m≤24m\leq 24. PCA recovers almost no modes at any mm (≤ 9%{\leq}\,9\%), as expected since its orthogonal components cannot align with non-orthogonal mode centroids. FastICA overtakes the SAE on alignment from m=48m=48 but recovers fewer modes at cosine ≥ 0.7{\geq}\,0.7 (Fig. 1). K-Means with a 512-component dictionary (not shown in Fig. 1) recovers more mode directions than the SAE at m≤48m\leq 48 but does not close the alignment gap: it underperforms the 75-component reference at every m≥32m\geq 32 on code–GT alignment (paired Wilcoxon p≈0.03p{\approx}0.03 at m≥48m\geq 48), so added capacity alone does not give K-Means the SAE’s per-user weight recovery. The soft-frozen decoder SAE of (Korznikov et al., 2026), their strongest baseline for feature recovery, tracks the SAE only at low mm where our setup enters Korznikov’s high-overcompleteness regime (dhidden/m≫1d_{\text{hidden}}/m\gg 1). Our real-data experiments sit at dhidden/m=4d_{\text{hidden}}/m=4 and omit this baseline. Frozen-encoder and frozen-decoder variants each fail on routing or direction recovery respectively outside this regime (Korznikov et al., 2026), so training both components is load-bearing at our overcompleteness.

Per-feature correlation reveals the feature splitting discussed in Section 3.1: raw SAE median r≈0.35r\approx 0.35 rises to ≈ 0.70{\approx}\,0.70 at m=128m{=}128 after merging, confirming the splitting is artifactual. With ground truth known, we can also analyze how monosemantic each feature is: for each mode we identify the feature that best ranks mode-positive users above mode-negative users (Precision among the top nposn_{\text{pos}}), and report the mean across modes. The merged SAE produces 1.41.4–2×2\times more monosemantic latents than K-Means encoding or raw embedding dimensions (0.530.53 vs. 0.390.39 and 0.280.28 at m=128m{=}128, using a separately trained 512-wide SAE on one projection). FastICA attains even higher per-feature monosemanticity (0.750.75) since the generative model’s independent-mode assumption exactly matches its objective, but with lower decoder-direction recovery at high cos thresholds (Fig. 1).

Transformer embeddings.

Eq. (2) holds only approximately for nonlinear encoders (see Section 3.1), so we repeat the experiment on embeddings from a trained sequence encoder: SASRec with the architecture and hyperparameters of our MovieLens encoder (see Appendix E.1), trained on the synthetic interaction sequences and mean-pooled into d=256d{=}256 user embeddings (see Appendix A.6). The oracle ceiling stays close to that of the mean-pooled product embeddings at the same dimension (0.780.78 vs. 0.850.85). The SAE leads every method on code–GT alignment (0.580.58, vs. 0.530.53 for FastICA, 0.450.45 for K-Means encoding, 0.370.37 for LDA fit to the raw user–item counts, and 0.250.25 for PCA) and recovers 73 of 75 modes at cosine ≥ 0.7{\geq}\,0.7, close to its 100%100\% on the mean-pooled embeddings, while FastICA and K-Means encoding drop from 95%95\% to 59%59\% and from 79%79\% to 52%52\%. The SAE also recovers more modes than PCA, FastICA, and K-Means encoding at every projected dimension m∈[16,128]m\in[16,128], keeps the best alignment when the encoder itself is trained at d=64<Kd{=}64<K, and captures a nearly constant 7373–75%75\% of the oracle ceiling as the number of modes varies from 15 to 75 (see Appendix A.6).

5 Behavioral Modes in Real World Data

We evaluate on two complementary datasets: Open e-commerce 1.0 (Berke et al., 2024) (1.8M purchases from 5027 U.S. consumers, with a self-reported life-event survey) and MovieLens 1M (Harper and Konstan, 2015) (1M ratings, 6040 users, 3706 movies). We use the same pipeline on both: generate user embeddings (method-specific, described in each subsection), train a sparse decomposition, and auto-interpret each latent with an LLM from its top-activating users. At query time, the feature interpretations are shown to an LLM alongside a natural-language audience query. The LLM scores each latent’s relevance on a 0–10 scale and we retain features scoring ≥5\geq 5. Users are then ranked by the weighted sum of their activations on the retained features. We use Claude Sonnet 4.6 for interpretation and Claude Haiku 4.5 for query-time feature scoring. Replacing the interpretation model with the open-weight Llama 3.3 70B on one Open e-commerce seed leaves SAE retrieval largely unchanged and keeps the SAE ahead of every baseline on mean Lift, with narrower margins over FastICA and K-Means encoding (see Appendix C.5).

Our primary method is a ReLU SAE with fixed L1 sparsity penalty and 4×4\times overcompleteness (width chosen per embedding, sparsity λ\lambda selected via the decoder-orthogonality criterion of (Chanin and Garriga-Alonso, 2025)).11 1 MovieLens embeddings are L2L_{2}-normalized and then standardized before SAE training, and Open e-commerce embeddings are used as produced. These steps preserve the form of Eq. (2) up to a per-user rescaling of the mode weights, a fixed linear map of the centroids, and a constant offset. As classical sparse alternatives we report K-Means encoding (defined in Section 4) and FastICA (the most competitive classical baseline on Open e-commerce), with PCA in Appendix B. We also report a text-embedding baseline as the natural zero-shot NL-retrieval alternative that requires no decomposition: we embed a per-user text summary and the NL query with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and rank by cosine similarity. The summary is a TF-IDF-weighted mean of sentence-transformer embeddings over purchased category names for Open e-commerce (matching the exact signal the SAE, K-Means, and ICA consume) and the mean of watched movie-title embeddings for MovieLens. For each task we report Lift@nposn_{\text{pos}}, AUROC, Coverage (fraction of positives with nonzero retrieval score), and FVU (fraction of embedding variance unexplained by the best linear decoder fit from the method’s codes); Lift, AUROC, and Coverage are averaged across tasks.

5.1 Open e-commerce

Setup.

We segment user order histories into 6-month windows, build per-window user-by-category count matrices over the 1864 categories with more than 5 purchases in any window, apply log scaling and TF-IDF weighting, L2L_{2}-normalize each row, and take truncated SVD to 128 dimensions. Apart from the log scaling and row normalization this embedding is linear in the category counts, so its structure approximately matches Eq. (2). The SAE is 4×4{\times} overcomplete (dhidden=512d_{\text{hidden}}{=}512) with mean L0≈23L_{0}{\approx}23 (Appendix C). Tasks split into (i) category retrieval (6 tasks spanning base rates 8 to 54%: pet owner, coffee enthusiast, gardener, board gamer, baby products, musician), where positives are users who purchased in the target categories in post-2021 windows, and (ii) life-event retrieval (new parent, moved residence), where positives are users who self-reported the life event in 2021.

Results.

SAE decomposition recovers the underlying behavioral modes faithfully enough to support zero-shot natural-language retrieval that matches or exceeds every classical sparse baseline on every retrieval-quality metric. SAE significantly exceeds K-Means encoding on every metric across both task blocks (cross-seed paired Wilcoxon, 5 seeds: all p≤0.009p{\leq}0.009; Appendix D) and PCA on every metric (all p<10−3p{<}10^{-3}). FastICA is the closest competitor: on category tasks SAE wins Lift (p=2×10−4p{=}2{\times}10^{-4}), AUROC (p=0.004p{=}0.004), and AUROCscored{}_{\text{scored}} (p=3×10−4p{=}3{\times}10^{-4}); on life-event tasks SAE wins Lift and AUROCscored{}_{\text{scored}} (p=0.001p{=}0.001 each) and ties on AUROC (p=0.5p{=}0.5, 0.7150.715 vs. 0.7130.713). ICA is higher on Coverage across both blocks (due to its denser activations). Against the text-embedding baseline, SAE wins on Lift and AUROC (Coverage is not a meaningful axis for this similarity-search baseline). SAE and ICA have the highest reconstruction fidelity (FVU 0.0750.075 vs. 0.0830.083); PCA and K-Means lag (0.360.36–0.390.39). Note that reconstruction quality does not always translate to retrieval performance: ICA matches SAE on FVU but trails on Lift (Table 8).

5.2 MovieLens 1M

Setup.

MovieLens 1M tests the nonlinear transformer-embedding regime where the superposition of Eq. (2) holds only approximately (see Section 3.1). To test encoder-architecture robustness we train two transformer recommenders on chronologically ordered interactions: SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018) (causal self-attention, next-item prediction) and BERT4Rec (Sun et al., 2019) (bidirectional self-attention, masked-item Cloze), both at dmodel=256d_{\text{model}}{=}256 with user embeddings obtained by mean-pooling final-layer hidden states. The SAE is 4×4\times overcomplete (dhidden=1024d_{\text{hidden}}{=}1024) with mean L0≈80L_{0}{\approx}80. Full SAE and transformer hyperparameters are in Appendix E.1. The decoder-orthogonality operating point (see Section 5) minimizes artifactual feature splitting in-training, so no post-hoc merging is applied on real data. Residual finer-grained latents under nonlinear FF are implicitly handled via the auto-interp confidence filter at retrieval (see Section 3.2). Features that track engagement intensity rather than taste are identified and relabeled as engagement-axis features before retrieval, uniformly across SAE and K-Means-encoding codes (Appendix E.6). We evaluate on 32 natural-language audience queries (21 broad, 11 niche, full list in Appendix E.2). Ground truth is generated by a deterministic title-pattern rule: for each query we curate a list of matching movie titles from the MovieLens catalog, optionally gated by a MovieLens genre constraint, and label a user positive if their watch history contains ≥3\geq 3 such titles.

Results.

At matched dictionary size (dhidden=1024d_{\text{hidden}}{=}1024) and matched L0L_{0}, SAE decomposition and K-Means encoding are matched on Lift and AUROC (cross-seed paired Wilcoxon p≥0.1p{\geq}0.1 on both encoders; Table 10). The SAE advantage is structural, and surfaces on three axes: coverage (98%98\% vs. 8181–85%85\% of true positives scored, p<10−4p{<}10^{-4} on both encoders), scored ranking (higher AUROCscored{}_{\text{scored}} on SASRec, p=0.014p{=}0.014, trending on BERT4Rec, p=0.07p{=}0.07), and reconstruction fidelity (9696–97%97\% of embedding variance recovered from SAE codes vs. 8686–89%89\% from K-Means codes). The text-embedding baseline reaches 100%100\% coverage by construction (it embeds every user’s watched-title history densely) and a comparable AUROC. Its Lift, which measures precision at the top of the ranking, is significantly below the SAE’s on both encoders (Stouffer p<10−3p{<}10^{-3}). These results are consistent across both transformer objectives (causal next-item and bidirectional masked). Because MovieLens ground truth is derived from titles, we also retrieve against 14 held-out self-reported demographic labels that no stage of the pipeline sees. The text-embedding baseline, which matched the SAE on AUROC for the title-derived tasks, falls to near-chance AUROC, significantly below the SAE, and its Lift remains well below the SAE’s (see Appendix E.3). The coverage advantage holds, and the Lift and AUROC differences with K-Means encoding stay small, at every auto-interpretation confidence threshold from 0.0 to 0.7 (see Appendix E.4).

The central MovieLens finding is not that SAE ranks better than K-Means. K-Means encoding is itself a sparse decomposition, and it retrieves competitively because the superposition structure is there for its centroids to approximate. At matched dictionary size and sparsity both methods saturate the same ranking signal, and the finding is structural: the SAE dictionary is near-orthogonal (pairwise decoder cosines centered at 0, mean absolute value 0.060.06 to 0.080.08 on SASRec), while K-Means centroids overlap (mean pairwise cosine 0.290.29 on SASRec, 0.170.17 on BERT4Rec, see Appendix E.1) and multiple centroids partition the same neighborhood. Overlapping centroids paraphrase one region of the embedding space and leave others uncovered, which costs coverage before it costs rank order, and the same geometry drives the feature-level redundancy in Section 5.3. On Open e-commerce, whose embedding is approximately linear, the same comparison favors the SAE on every retrieval metric (see Section 5.1). On broad queries against a saturated ranking signal, we do not expect ranking gains from orthogonality alone.

5.3 Audience characterization

A second application of the decomposition is audience characterization: given a behaviorally-defined audience, surface the features that best describe it. A useful top-kk feature set should span distinct explanatory concepts rather than paraphrase a single concept, and should cover the target audience under semantically-grounded selection. On 20 franchise-level audiences in MovieLens-1M at k=5k{=}5, the SAE top-kk features are significantly less redundant than the matched-L0L_{0} K-Means-encoding top-kk (Stouffer p≈4×10−4p{\approx}4{\times}10^{-4}) and cover significantly more of the target audience under reverse-selector ranking (Stouffer p≈10−7p{\approx}10^{-7}, see Appendix D). Within confidence-filtered features (≥0.6\geq 0.6) that surface the same niche audience, K-Means encoding allocates 2.2×2.2\times more features per distinct concept than SAE (2.202.20 vs 1.001.00 redundancy ratio, averaged across 5 niche audiences; Appendix E.5). The effect is even more pronounced on Open e-commerce’s approximately linear embeddings (2.822.82 vs 1.141.14, or 2.5×2.5\times, see Appendix E.5), as anticipated by our generative framework. The K-Means reference has higher per-feature lift but narrower per-feature activation distributions, so its redundant top-kk does not translate into better audience coverage. Figure 2 illustrates on the Jurassic Park audience. See Appendix E.5 for the full protocol and the reverse-selector definition.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we extended the superposition hypothesis for learned representations to user embeddings, arguing that both classical (linear) and deep-learning user embeddings decompose into sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes recoverable by sparse autoencoders. Empirical feature-level analysis supports the framework: for both transformer encoders on MovieLens, SAE decompositions produce more behaviorally distinct features than the strongest classical baseline. On synthetic data, SAEs recover more known ground-truth modes than classical decomposition methods, and this holds for transformer-encoded embeddings as well. On the mean-pooled synthetic embeddings, a fixed post-hoc merging procedure approximately restores the mode granularity assumed by the generative model despite overcomplete feature splitting. On two real-world datasets, the resulting decompositions enabled natural-language audience retrieval over embeddings never trained on text. Because the method is post-hoc and model-agnostic, it applies to any pre-trained embedding without modifying the upstream system.

More broadly, behavioral mode decomposition provides a general-purpose lens for understanding what user embeddings encode. This has practical implications for auditing recommendation systems, surfacing what behavioral signals drive personalization, and giving practitioners transparent, queryable representations of their user base. The same capability carries privacy risk. Making an embedding queryable in natural language lowers the cost of inferring sensitive traits, such as recent life events, and extends it to anyone holding the embeddings and the interaction histories of the example users shown during interpretation. Because the recovered features are enumerable and named, sensitive directions can also be detected, excluded, or ablated, which is not possible with a dense embedding.

Several extensions remain open. We considered at most two temporal snapshots per user, but behavioral modes evolve, and their temporal dynamics may signal shifts in preference or life circumstance. Our weighted-sum combinator handles additive concept overlap but not logical constraints or temporal sequencing (e.g., “viewers who shifted from A to B”). Explicit combinators over mode directions are a natural next step. We also experimented only with ReLU SAEs, and other SAE variants and sparse dictionary learning algorithms remain to be tested. Both real-world datasets represent consumption domains with positive-only interaction sequences, and both deep encoders are transformer sequential recommenders (SASRec, BERT4Rec). Domains with different interaction semantics (e.g., mobility or explicit negative feedback) and other deep-learning architectures (e.g., MLP or CNN encoders) remain to be tested. Finally, recent work identifies persona-like structure in LLM internal states via linear probing (Chen et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). Our results suggest SAE-based recovery may discover richer persona structure post-hoc, particularly when persona directions are non-orthogonal or overcomplete.
