Appendix A Synthetic data experiments

This appendix comprises additional details regarding the synthetic data experiments of Sec. 4.

A.1 Setup

In this experiment, we generate synthetic user–product interactions based on ground truth behavioral modes and test the extent to which various methods can recover them from the embeddings alone. Each ground-truth behavioral mode 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} is defined by a name, description, product categories, and example products, with an occurrence frequency πk\pi_{k} governing its prevalence. We prompted Claude Opus 4.6 to generate K=75K{=}75 such modes spanning five domains (Technology & Gaming, Fitness & Outdoors, Home & Kitchen, Lifestyle & Hobbies, Family & Personal Care). The resulting set of behavioral modes is shown in Table 4. With the behavioral modes defined, we generate 100,000 synthetic user shopping histories. For each user 𝒰\mathcal{U}, we sample a number of active behavioral modes n𝒰∼Pois⁡(λ=2)+2n_{\mathcal{U}}\sim\mathrm{Pois}(\lambda=2)+2, clipped so that n𝒰∈[2,6]n_{\mathcal{U}}\in[2,6]. The specific n𝒰n_{\mathcal{U}} modes are chosen randomly from the set of all behavioral modes with probability proportional to the popularities πk\pi_{k}, and their weights are drawn independently from LogNormal⁡(0,0.5)\mathrm{LogNormal}(0,0.5) and normalized to sum to one. We inject noise into the purchase history with weight sampled uniformly from [0.05,0.2][0.05,0.2]. The total number of orders per user is drawn from a log-normal distribution with underlying-normal parameters μ=4\mu=4 and σ=0.8\sigma=0.8 (median e4≈55e^{4}\approx 55 interactions), clipped to [10,300][10,300]. We allocate the corresponding fraction of interactions to each mode weight plus the noise weight, requiring at least one interaction per active behavioral mode. The generation token budget truncates the longest histories, so realized histories have at most 108 orders (see Appendix A.2).

To generate synthetic user embeddings, we then pass the 100,000 synthetic user profiles described above to Claude Sonnet 4 to generate a corresponding product interaction history for each user. The history generated consists of product names related to each represented behavioral mode. For noise, we provide a list of example product categories and have it inject similar products. Finally, the user embedding is generated by embedding each of the product names in a user’s history with a word embedding model, all-mpnet-base-v2, and taking their mean. Histories parsed successfully for 99,832 users, with 5,803,030 interactions in total. This results in a 768-dimensional dense embedding for each user that is inherently a superposition of underlying behavioral modes. We L2L_{2}-normalize and standardize these embeddings, project them onto random directions in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} following [Bingham and Mannila, 2001] to vary the amount of superposition, and then standardize and L2L_{2}-normalize the projected embeddings.

A.2 Data statistics

Table 3 and Figure 3 compare item popularity and user activity in the synthetic data with both real datasets. The synthetic data is more head-concentrated than either real dataset, with the top 1% of items carrying 51% of interactions, and its fraction of singleton items lies between theirs. Below the median, synthetic user activity resembles MovieLens, while Open e-commerce has more low-activity users (p50/p10 activity ratio 2.89, vs. 3.56 for MovieLens and 6.63 for Open e-commerce). Above the median, the generation budget truncates the synthetic upper tail near twice the median. The synthetic data therefore reproduces the short head and long tail of item popularity that characterize real-world user interaction data. This implies the recovery results of Section 4 do not depend on unrealistically uniform item popularity. The synthetic data distribution differs from the real-world examples considered primarily by lacking very heavy users.

A.3 SAE and other baselines

For the SAE, we take the vanilla ReLU version described in Eq. (3), with an adaptive λ\lambda sparsity penalty to match the ground truth L0L_{0}. Here, λ\lambda is warmed up for 10 epochs, then log⁡λ\log\lambda is adjusted each epoch by an amount proportional to the difference between current and target L0L_{0}. The SAE has dhidden=300d_{\text{hidden}}=300 and is trained for 50 epochs with batch size 256 and learning rate 10−310^{-3}.

We consider six additional baselines: random projections onto 300 unit vectors (the SAE’s width) with ReLU, sparsified versions of PCA and FastICA, K-Means encoding (cosine similarity to K-Means centroids passed through ReLU and thresholded to match the ground-truth L0L_{0}, following [Coates and Ng, 2012]), the soft-frozen decoder SAE of [Korznikov et al., 2026], and NMF on shifted (non-negative) embeddings. K-Means encoding uses 75 components matching the ground-truth mode count, and PCA, ICA, and NMF use min⁡(75,m)\min(75,m). The soft-frozen decoder uses identical hyperparameters to the SAE. To ensure fair comparison, we sparsify all non-SAE methods except NMF to match the ground-truth mean L0L_{0} by zeroing activations below a calibrated threshold. NMF retains its natural sparsity, as we find additional thresholding degrades its performance. Note that every time we report results on these methods, they correspond to the sparsified versions.

A.4 Mode recovery at other cosine thresholds

The conclusions of Figure 1 do not hinge on the 0.7 cosine cutoff for mode recovery. Repeating the evaluation at thresholds from 0.5 to 0.8, the SAE recovers more modes than FastICA, PCA, and NMF at every threshold and every mm, and more than every classical baseline in Figure 1 for m≥32m\geq 32. At m≤24m\leq 24, K-Means encoding matches the SAE at 0.7 (m=16m=16) and exceeds it at 0.8, but its recovery does not improve with dimension (0.690.69 to 0.740.74 at 0.8 across all mm), whereas the SAE’s rises from 0.470.47 at m=16m=16 to 0.980.98 at m=128m=128 and overtakes it from m=32m=32. K-Means centroids thus capture a fixed fraction of the modes regardless of how much room the embedding leaves to separate them, while the SAE uses the additional dimensions.

A.5 Soft-frozen-decoder baseline

Korznikov et al. [2026] point out that SAEs can fail to learn the underlying features from LLM activations, with performance matched or exceeded by simple random baselines in high-dimensional regimes. To check whether this equivalence holds in our setup, we train a soft-frozen-decoder variant alongside the standard SAE [Korznikov et al., 2026]. The soft-frozen variant uses identical hyperparameters to the fully trained SAE (adaptive L1L_{1} to match ground-truth average L0L_{0}, same learning rate and starting λ\lambda), so any divergence between the two isolates the contribution of decoder training.

A.6 Transformer embeddings of the synthetic data

To test recovery when the embedding is produced by a trained sequence encoder, we train SASRec with the MovieLens configuration of Appendix E.1 (dmodel=256d_{\text{model}}{=}256, 4 heads, 2 layers, max_len=200\texttt{max\_len}{=}200, dropout 0.30.3, learning rate 5×10−45{\times}10^{-4}) on the synthetic interaction sequences. Items are normalized product names that appear at least 5 times (119,826 items covering 83.9% of interactions, 99,213 users), and each user’s history is shuffled, since the generative model draws interactions independently. The encoder reaches a test HR@10 of 0.93. User embeddings are the mean of final-layer hidden states, standardized and L2L_{2}-normalized, and the SAE (dhidden=300d_{\text{hidden}}{=}300) and baselines are run exactly as in Section 4. Items are not mode-exclusive: 15 to 20% of interaction mass falls on noise items bought across modes, and the mass-weighted mode purity over all items is 0.74 (1.0 would be perfectly exclusive).

Table 6 reports recovery at d=256d{=}256. A linear readout still recovers most of the mode information (oracle 0.780.78, vs. 0.850.85 for the mean-pooled product embeddings at m=256m{=}256), so the encoder preserves the modes, and the SAE recovers them best. It leads on code–GT alignment and recovers 73 of 75 modes at cosine ≥ 0.7{\geq}\,0.7 (97 to 100% across repeated SAE trainings on the same embeddings), while the classical baselines lose much more relative to the mean-pooled case, FastICA falling from 95%95\% to 59%59\% recovery. FastICA keeps the highest per-feature correlation, as in Section 4, and merging raises the SAE’s from 0.280.28 to 0.540.54. Per-mode recovery correlates with the fraction of a mode’s interactions that survives the vocabulary threshold (Spearman ρ=0.31\rho=0.31). LDA, fit to the raw user–item counts with 75 topics and sparsified to the same L0L_{0}, recovers real structure but trails the SAE on both metrics it supports, consistent with the claim in Section 2 that embeddings carry more recoverable mode structure than raw counts. Doubling its training iterations changes its alignment by less than 0.010.01.

The same picture holds under further compression and when the encoder itself must superpose the modes. Randomly projecting the d=256d{=}256 embeddings to m=16m=16 to 128128 (5 projections each), the SAE recovers more modes than PCA, FastICA, and K-Means encoding at every mm, although FastICA attains higher alignment for m≥48m\geq 48. An encoder trained at dmodel=64<Kd_{\text{model}}{=}64<K has a lower ceiling (oracle 0.580.58), yet the SAE still has the best alignment (0.410.41, vs. 0.360.36 for FastICA) and recovers 97%97\% of modes at cosine ≥ 0.5{\geq}\,0.5 and 71%71\% at ≥ 0.7{\geq}\,0.7, while FastICA recovers none at either threshold. Finally, Table 7 varies the number of modes. Restricting the population to users whose active modes all lie among the K′K^{\prime} most popular modes gives exact K′K^{\prime}-mode ground truth, and the SAE (with dhidden=4​K′d_{\text{hidden}}=4K^{\prime}) captures a nearly constant 7373 to 75%75\% of the oracle ceiling while matching or exceeding the best classical baseline at every K′K^{\prime}. The restriction selects users with fewer and more concentrated modes, which is why we report the oracle-normalized ratio, and K′=10K^{\prime}=10 leaves too few users (2,043) to evaluate.

Appendix B Additional baselines: PCA, ICA

The main text reports SAE (primary) and K-Means encoding on both datasets, plus FastICA on Open e-commerce (its closest classical competitor). For completeness, Table 8 reports PCA and FastICA on both datasets at matched mean L0L_{0}. PCA and ICA are capped at the input dimension by construction (d=128d{=}128 on Open e-commerce, d=256d{=}256 on MovieLens), since orthogonal/independent components cannot be overcomplete. SAE and K-Means encoding use the SAE’s dictionary width (dhidden=512d_{\text{hidden}}{=}512 for Open e-commerce, dhidden=1024d_{\text{hidden}}{=}1024 for MovieLens). Numbers are averaged across tasks within each dataset.

Appendix C Open e-commerce additional details

C.1 Embedding generation

Embeddings are generated by segmenting user order histories into 6-month chunks, constructing the user-category count matrix on each chunk (1864 categories with > 5{>}\,5 purchases in any window), applying log scaling and TF-IDF weighting, L2L_{2}-normalizing each row, and taking truncated SVD with embedding dimension 128. The SAE is trained directly on these embeddings. No text input enters the decomposition pipeline at any point. We select the SAE operating point following the decoder-orthogonality criterion of [Chanin and Garriga-Alonso, 2025], giving dhidden=512d_{\text{hidden}}{=}512 (4×4{\times} overcomplete), λ=5×10−4\lambda{=}5\times 10^{-4}, 25 epochs, and mean L0≈23L_{0}{\approx}23. All 512 latents remain live after training (no dead features). We use Claude Sonnet 4.6 to auto-interpret each latent, passing 10 high-activating positives and 10 random negatives and asking the model to identify the behavioral pattern present in the positives and absent in the negatives, producing a short feature name (e.g., “Premium_Dog_Food_Buyers”) and one-sentence description. Full prompts are in Appendix F. Reported retrieval numbers are averaged over 5 SAE training seeds with the same operating point, and cross-seed paired Wilcoxon tests are reported in Appendix D.

C.2 Tasks and ground truth

We consider 6 category retrieval tasks spanning base rates 8–54% (pet owner, coffee enthusiast, gardener, board gamer, baby products, musician), and 2 life-event retrieval tasks from the companion survey (new parent in 2021, moved residence in 2021). Other survey life events (e.g., divorced, changed jobs) either had insufficient positive counts or did not correlate with category-level behavior changes, and are excluded. Early in experimentation we considered two additional category tasks (Fisher, Photographer) for which the retrieval pipeline’s default gating settings did not allow any features through for at least one method; per-method retuning would eliminate the zero-return behavior, but we instead fix the operating point across methods for apples-to-apples comparison of feature and interpretation quality. For category tasks, positives are users who purchased in the target categories in post-2021 windows; we use the dataset’s canonical category definitions for each task (listed in Table 9). For life-event tasks, positives are users who self-reported the event in 2021.

C.3 Retrieval strategies

SAE + NL (main-text primary) presents all feature interpretations to an LLM alongside a natural-language audience query, which scores each feature’s relevance on a 0–10 scale; we retain features scoring ≥5\geq 5 and rank users by the weighted sum of their activations on the retained features. This strategy is fully zero-shot: it sees only the NL query and the feature interpretations.

K-Means encoding + NL uses the same scoring and ranking pipeline, substituting K-Means-encoding features for SAE features.

Text-embedding baseline requires no sparse decomposition. For each user we embed the NL query with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and rank users by cosine similarity to a per-user text vector. The user vector is the category-pooled variant: a TF-IDF-weighted mean of sentence-transformer embeddings over the user’s purchased category names (with underscores replaced by spaces and lowercased so the encoder receives natural-language phrases). This is the matched-input fair comparison: the SAE, K-Means encoding, and ICA consume exactly the same TF-IDF-weighted category signal, so any retrieval advantage over this baseline is attributable to the decomposition itself rather than to extra text the baseline did not see.

Raw category counts ranks users by their pre-2021 purchase counts in each task’s target categories. It is an oracle for the category-retrieval block (it uses the ground-truth category definition) and a category-based approximation for the life-event block (using hand-picked proxy categories such as diapers/baby food for “new parent”). We include it as a ceiling, not as a comparison target.

SAE + correlation (reported here for completeness only; not zero-shot) selects the 20 SAE features most correlated with target-category purchases in pre-2021 data, then ranks users by their weighted activations on those features. This requires access to the target category list for each task and is therefore not a zero-shot method. We report its numbers as a reference point for how much signal the SAE features carry when supervised feature selection is applied.

C.4 Task-type breakdown

Category-retrieval tasks.

Aggregate 5-seed means are in Table 1; cross-seed p-values are in Table 10. A supervised SAE+correlation variant selects the 20 SAE features most correlated with per-task target-category purchases in pre-2021 data and ranks users by weighted activation on those features. This variant is not zero-shot and requires the per-task category list that SAE+NL does not see. At matched L0L_{0} it reaches mean Lift@nposn_{\text{pos}} of ≈1.9×{\approx}1.9\times and mean AUROC of ≈0.72{\approx}0.72, roughly matching the zero-shot SAE+NL variant on both. The SAE dictionary therefore contains enough per-task signal to recover supervised-ranking quality from unsupervised decomposition alone.

Life-event tasks.

The category-counts column here is a keyword-proxy, not an oracle: past purchases of hand-picked proxy categories (diapers, baby food) do not pre-identify users who will become parents, and no comparable proxy list exists for residential mobility. SAE+NL beats K-Means encoding and PCA on Lift, AUROC, and AUROCscored{}_{\text{scored}} with cross-seed p=0.001p{=}0.001 (10 paired seed–task observations; Table 10). Against ICA, SAE wins Lift and AUROCscored{}_{\text{scored}} (p=0.001p{=}0.001–0.0020.002) and ties on AUROC (p=0.5p{=}0.5, 0.7150.715 vs. 0.7130.713). ICA achieves higher Coverage than SAE on both tasks due to its denser activations, mirroring the category-task pattern.

C.5 Open-weight interpretation model

We chose Claude Sonnet 4.6 for interpretation because it was among the strongest models at its scale and was available for large-scale batch inference on our platform. To test whether the retrieval results depend on the interpretation model, we re-name the features of one Open e-commerce seed with the open-weight Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (via Amazon Bedrock, temperature 0), holding everything else fixed: the same SAE and baseline codes, the same sampled users and prompts, and the same Claude Haiku 4.5 query-time scoring. Llama’s names closely track Sonnet’s. The median sentence-embedding cosine between the two models’ name-and-description strings for the same feature is 0.64 to 0.69 across methods, against 0.29 to 0.35 for different features. Llama assigns nearly constant confidence scores (0.92±0.010.92\pm 0.01), so the 0.6 confidence filter passes every feature, and we therefore also evaluate Llama’s names paired with Sonnet’s confidence scores. In both variants the SAE remains ahead of every baseline on mean Lift in both task blocks, and its own Lift stays within 6% of the Sonnet-named value on at least 6 of the 8 tasks. Its margins over FastICA and K-Means encoding narrow, however. With Llama’s names, the SAE’s category-task AUROC lead over K-Means encoding falls from 0.031 to under 0.01, and its life-event Lift lead over FastICA from 0.32 to about 0.03. For scale, re-running query-time scoring on the Sonnet names alone changes Lift by up to 0.012 on category tasks and 0.09 on life-event tasks, since the scoring is not fully deterministic. The direction of the comparison therefore does not depend on the interpretation model, but its size partly does. Llama’s names lead the query-time gate to admit more features per query for every method (21 vs. 14 for the SAE), which raises the baselines’ coverage (K-Means encoding on category tasks, 0.61 to 0.75) while the SAE’s barely changes. Part of the SAE’s margin under Sonnet thus comes from how features are named and selected rather than from the decomposition alone. This replication uses a single seed and no significance test.

Appendix D Statistical significance tables

Table 10 consolidates all Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Stouffer combinations referenced in the main text. All tests are one-sided with alternative hypothesis SAE >> baseline. The direction is pre-specified by the hypothesis, not chosen after observing the data. For tests where the baseline wins we report the reverse-direction pp-value rather than suppressing the comparison.

Open e-commerce tests are paired across 5 seeds ×\times task (6 category tasks or 2 life-event tasks) as cross-seed paired observations. MovieLens retrieval tests are paired across the 32 non-compositional NL audience queries, reported separately per encoder and Stouffer-combined. Audience-characterization tests are paired across 20 franchise audiences, Stouffer-combined across the two MovieLens encoders.

Appendix E MovieLens additional details

E.1 Width-and-sparsity sweep

Transformer recommenders.

SASRec [Kang and McAuley, 2018] and BERT4Rec [Sun et al., 2019] both use dmodel=256d_{\text{model}}{=}256, 4 heads, 2 layers, max_len=200\texttt{max\_len}{=}200, dropout 0.30.3, learning rate 5×10−45{\times}10^{-4}, trained on chronologically ordered interactions. User embeddings are the mean of non-padding final-layer hidden states.

SAE operating point.

We selected the SAE operating point reported in Section 5.2 using the decoder-orthogonality criterion of [Chanin and Garriga-Alonso, 2025]: we sweep λ\lambda at a fixed width and pick the elbow of mean pairwise decoder cosine similarity (cdecc_{\text{dec}}). Among widths satisfying this elbow condition, we choose the smallest width that maintains a high absolute count of features with sufficient statistical support for reliable auto-interpretation (30–500 activating users, “eligible” in what follows). Our final choice is dhidden=1024d_{\text{hidden}}{=}1024 with λ=1.98×10−3\lambda{=}1.98{\times}10^{-3}. The same λ\lambda is used for both encoders. Measured L0L_{0} differs only slightly (≈80{\approx}80 on SASRec, ≈83{\approx}83 on BERT4Rec), giving a direct architecture-level comparison at a matched sparsity target.

Width and sparsity.

Table 11 reports representative rows of the sweep on SASRec embeddings at dhidden=1024d_{\text{hidden}}{=}1024. cdecc_{\text{dec}} flattens for L0∈[65,100]L_{0}\in[65,100], indicating an elbow beyond which additional sparsity pressure does not further improve decoder orthogonality. Within this band, L0≈80L_{0}{\approx}80 maximizes eligible feature count. The same qualitative picture holds for BERT4Rec embeddings. Widths below 1024 (d∈{256,512}d{\in}\{256,512\}) cap eligible-feature yield at under 30% and were ruled out; d=2048d{=}2048 exhibited high dead-feature counts without improving either metric.

Decoder-cosine distributions.

Pairwise decoder cosines are centered near zero for the SAE on both encoders (mean 0.00010.0001 on SASRec, 0.00080.0008 on BERT4Rec), confirming the near-orthogonal geometry claimed in Section 5.2. K-Means encoding’s centroids are natively denser (mean pairwise cosine 0.290.29 on SASRec, 0.170.17 on BERT4Rec).

Training length.

Table 12 reports a training-length sensitivity check at the selected (d,λ)(d,\lambda) configuration. Training past 250 epochs begins to over-sparsify the dictionary: eligible-feature count declines as features slip below the 30-user support threshold, and cdecc_{\text{dec}} worsens because the dying features leave behind overlapping decoder directions. Shorter training (125 epochs) produces a higher raw eligible count, but inspection of the top features reveals within-theme redundancy (e.g. multiple distinct “classic Western” latents) that an overcomplete dictionary has not yet deduplicated. We therefore train to 250 epochs for both encoders, which sits at the inflection point between under- and over-training.

E.2 Natural-language audience queries and ground truth

Table 13 lists the 32 non-compositional natural-language audience queries used in the MovieLens retrieval evaluation, along with the title patterns and optional MovieLens-genre constraint used to resolve each query to a ground-truth positive set. Ground-truth labels are generated by a deterministic rule: for query QQ with title-pattern set 𝒫Q\mathcal{P}_{Q} and optional genre constraint 𝒢Q\mathcal{G}_{Q}, a user is labelled positive if their MovieLens watch history contains ≥3\geq 3 movies whose title matches any pattern in 𝒫Q\mathcal{P}_{Q} (case-insensitive substring match) and whose MovieLens-listed genres include every genre in 𝒢Q\mathcal{G}_{Q}. Queries yielding fewer than 20 positive users in the evaluated population are dropped from the benchmark. One such dropped query, “viewers who enjoy martial arts and kung fu films”, falls below the floor on MovieLens 1M and is excluded. The remaining 32 are retained. Queries split into 21 broad audiences (e.g. Tarantino fans, Disney animation) and 11 niche audiences (e.g. French New Wave, pre-1960 film noir). Draft query strings and candidate title-pattern lists were generated with Claude Opus 4.6 and then curated by the authors against the MovieLens 1M catalog. The final patterns used to produce ground-truth labels are those listed in Table 13. Paired Wilcoxon p-values for per-query SAE-vs-baseline comparisons are consolidated in Appendix D, Table 10.

The text-embedding baseline evaluated alongside SAE and K-Means encoding scores each user by the cosine similarity between the query embedding and the user’s mean-pooled watched-title embedding (both computed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2).

Paired Wilcoxon p-values for MovieLens retrieval are consolidated in Appendix D, Table 10, alongside the Open e-commerce and audience-characterization tests. The headline conclusions for MovieLens: SAE and K-Means encoding are statistically indistinguishable on Lift@nposn_{\text{pos}} and AUROC. SAE wins Coverage by a large and highly significant margin on both encoders. SAE beats the text-embedding baseline on Lift but is nominally tied on AUROC, consistent with the text baseline’s dense-by-construction coverage giving it a full-population comparison set. The AUROCscored{}_{\text{scored}} column of Table 2 restricts to users each method actually scored, which leaves the text baseline slightly ahead on this metric.

E.3 Held-out demographic labels

Because MovieLens ground truth is derived from titles, which the auto-interpretation prompt also shows, retrieval could in principle reflect LLM title matching rather than the decomposition. As a control, we retrieve against all 14 of MovieLens’s self-reported demographic labels (age, gender, and occupation groups), which no stage of the pipeline sees, changing nothing else. The SAE reaches AUROC 0.58 (SASRec) and 0.60 (BERT4Rec) and Lift 2.00 and 2.06, against AUROC 0.54 and Lift 1.28 for the text-embedding baseline (one-sided paired Wilcoxon on AUROC over query and seed, p≤3×10−4p\leq 3{\times}10^{-4}). K-Means encoding also exceeds the text baseline, so the effect reflects sparse decomposition rather than our SAE specifically. If the benchmark measured title matching, both methods would degrade together. Instead, only the method that depends on item text does.

E.4 Sensitivity to the confidence threshold

The auto-interpretation confidence filter (≥ 0.6{\geq}\,0.6, cf. Section 3.2) removes about a third of SAE features on MovieLens but only a tenth of K-Means features, because the LLM assigns the broader K-Means features higher confidence. Table 14 re-runs retrieval at thresholds from 0.0 (no filter) to 0.7. Across this range, the Lift and AUROC differences between the SAE and K-Means encoding stay small, and the SAE maintains its advantage in coverage, which grows with the threshold. The threshold therefore acts as a resolution parameter rather than a tuned setting.

E.5 Audience characterization: protocol and statistics

We evaluate at matched k=5k{=}5 feature budget and a 10%10\% top-activator threshold per feature (matching the auto-interpretation sampling convention) on 20 franchise-level audiences in MovieLens-1M (≥2\geq 2 franchise films per user, ≥30\geq 30 users per audience). The K-Means-encoding reference is thresholded to match the SAE’s mean L0L_{0}, following Section 5.

Top-kk diversity.

Per audience, we rank features by lift and compute top-kk redundancy as the median pairwise cosine between BGE-large-en-v1.5 [Xiao et al., 2023] embeddings of the top-kk features’ {feature_name, feature_description} strings (lower cosine = less redundant, more diverse). We use BGE rather than the retrieval-standard MiniLM here because BGE provides finer paraphrase-discrimination needed for this metric, which specifically targets near-paraphrases that retrieval-tuned encoders collapse by design. The SAE decomposition yields a significantly less redundant top-5 than K-Means encoding on both encoders (SASRec K-Means −- SAE median cosine Δ=0.066\Delta{=}0.066, p=0.002p{=}0.002; BERT4Rec Δ=0.032\Delta{=}0.032, p=0.049p{=}0.049; Stouffer p≈4×10−4p{\approx}4{\times}10^{-4}, one-sided paired Wilcoxon with alternative K-Means>>SAE, across 20 audiences).

Reverse-selector audience coverage.

To probe whether redundancy costs audience coverage rather than being a free diversity bonus, we reverse the feature selector: we rank features by on-topic cosine similarity between their {name, description} and an LLM-generated audience description, take the top-5, then measure the fraction of each audience’s top-activators covered by the selected top-5. The SAE top-5 covers significantly more of the target audience (SASRec Δ=0.011\Delta{=}0.011, p=0.0003p{=}0.0003; BERT4Rec Δ=0.017\Delta{=}0.017, p=0.0001p{=}0.0001; Stouffer p≈10−7p{\approx}10^{-7}). The K-Means-encoding reference has higher per-feature lift but narrower per-feature activation distributions, so its redundant top-5 does not translate into better audience coverage. The SAE’s L1-sparsity and overcomplete dictionary produce a decomposition in which each selected direction contributes a distinct explanation of behavior — the property this task actually rewards.

Feature-level redundancy diagnostic.

The top-kk-diversity effect above has a feature-level structural account. For each of the 10 curated niche audiences in Appendix E.2 with npositive≤500n_{\text{positive}}{\leq}500, we identify SAE and K-Means features whose top-50 activators overlap the audience’s positive set (Jaccard≥0.05{\geq}0.05) and whose LLM interpretation confidence is ≥0.6{\geq}0.6 (matching the retrieval pipeline’s filter). Among these features, we compute pairwise activation Pearson correlation and an effective-concept count by agglomerative clustering at correlation threshold 0.50.5. The redundancy ratio is features per effective concept. Across the 5 niche audiences where both methods have ≥2{\geq}2 confidence-passing matched features (documentary, David Lynch, 1930s–40s screwball, French New Wave, Italian neorealism), SAE has mean activation correlation 0.160.16 vs K-Means 0.290.29, and a redundancy ratio of 1.001.00 vs 2.202.20. K-Means features that surface a single audience decompose into 22–44 redundant partitions per effective concept; SAE features are structurally distinct even when multiple features co-surface the same audience.

Open e-commerce feature-level redundancy.

Applying the same diagnostic to the SVD-on-counts SAE, with category audiences as ground truth and a precision-≥0.70\geq 0.70 match criterion (audience sizes of 300300–22002200 make Jaccard-based matching saturate at low values), we find the effect becomes more pronounced: SAE mean activation correlation 0.090.09 vs K-Means 0.330.33, redundancy ratio 1.141.14 vs 2.822.82 across 44/77 audiences with ≥2{\geq}2 matched features per method. 93%93\% of active SAE features pass the confidence filter (vs 65%65\% on MovieLens), consistent with the cleaner mode-to-feature alignment predicted for linear embedding functions in Section 3.1.

E.6 Volume-axis relabeling

A sparse decomposition of sequence-encoder embeddings can produce features that track engagement intensity (total films watched, recency of activity) rather than any taste pattern. Because such features fire on users with high activity regardless of content preference, they inflate retrieval lift on any audience query that correlates with engagement volume — for example, broad “fans of Hollywood films” queries where the positive set is dominated by heavy watchers.

We identify these features via a length-matched taste-free control: for each feature, we compare the content profile of its top activators against a group of non-activating users whose viewing counts match the activators’ volume distribution. A feature is classified as pure volume if the content profiles are statistically indistinguishable (no genre or era is significantly enriched in the activator group relative to the length-matched control at p<0.05p{<}0.05 after multiple-testing correction). Pure-volume features are relabeled from their auto-interpreted name to a single engagement-axis label (“heavy-watcher engagement axis”) before retrieval. The same detection procedure is applied to SAE and K-Means-encoding codes, ensuring both methods receive the same treatment.

Relabeled engagement features contribute to retrieval only to the extent that the LLM selects them based on semantic match to the query text. The protocol therefore ensures that broad audience queries correlated with viewing volume are not spuriously boosted by engagement features; the features remain available in the dictionary but are interpreted honestly as an engagement axis rather than a taste.

Appendix F Auto-interpretation and retrieval prompts

This section lists the LLM prompt templates used at each stage of the pipeline. We use Claude Sonnet 4.6 for feature interpretation (the offline, one-time auto-interp stage) and Claude Haiku 4.5 for query-time feature scoring. The key prompt elements of each stage are summarized below.

F.1 Feature interpretation (auto-interp)

For each SAE / baseline latent, we sample 10 top-activating users (positives) and 10 random non-activating users (negatives). For Open e-commerce we show per-window purchase-category summaries; for MovieLens we show a structured per-user behavioral summary (separately cached; see Appendix F.2 for the summary prompt used). The interpretation prompt varies by dataset to match what the underlying embedding can encode:

Open e-commerce (categories mode, SVD-on-counts embeddings).

The prompt instructs the model that the embedding is a TF-IDF-weighted SVD of user-by-category purchase counts in 6-month windows, and therefore encodes only which categories a user bought and roughly how often. It forbids brand-, title-, price-, or cadence-level claims, since the SAE cannot see them. The model is asked to infer who these people are (life-stage / lifestyle / household persona) from category combinations, at a granularity matched to the feature’s sparsity (common features →\to broader personas; rare features →\to specific personas). Output is a JSON object with feature_name, feature_description, confidence_score, and per-pattern reasoning. An enrichment context precomputed over the top-activating users’ windows (top categories with lift >2×>2\times vs. population) is supplied alongside the per-window examples to anchor the LLM on population-distinctive categories.

MovieLens (titles mode, transformer embeddings).

The prompt instructs the model that each positive is a user’s behavioral summary computed from their viewing history. The model is asked to identify the specific taste pattern that distinguishes positives from negatives, drawing on title semantics, genre mix, era, and co-viewing patterns that the sequence encoder can encode. Output is the same JSON schema.

Key design choices: (i) system prompt forbids hallucinated attributes for the embedding modality, (ii) positives and negatives are presented with matched formatting so the model cannot detect class via superficial cues, (iii) confidence scores below 0.60.6 are excluded from downstream retrieval.

F.2 MovieLens behavioral-summary prompt

Before auto-interpretation, each MovieLens user is summarized via a one-shot LLM call (Claude Sonnet 4.6) on their chronological watch history. The summary is cached per user and reused across all SAE / baseline auto-interp passes.

System prompt.

“You are a careful analyst producing structured behavioral summaries from movie watching histories. Base all claims only on the data shown. Do not invent patterns the history does not support.”

User prompt.

Per-user, the prompt supplies the chronologically ordered watch history (up to 150 items; title + release year + genres), basic stats (total count, earliest/latest release year), and instructs the model to produce six terse sections: (i) Volume and engagement (HEAVY/MODERATE/CASUAL classification against a 150-film MovieLens median), (ii) Era profile (decade-level release-year distribution with approximate fractions), (iii) Genre profile (top 5–7 genres with fractions), (iv) Stylistic/thematic tendencies (2–5 specific patterns, avoiding vague labels), (v) Director/franchise affinity (directors with ≥3{\geq}3 films or clear franchise patterns), (vi) Avoidances (genres/eras notably absent). The prompt explicitly forbids the model from inferring time-viewing rates or absolute viewing dates, since MovieLens does not include viewing timestamps and release years only bracket the films themselves.

F.3 Query-time feature scoring

Given an NL audience query, the retrieval pipeline asks the LLM to score each interpreted feature’s relevance to the query on a 0–10 scale. The prompt shows the query and a batch of {feature_name, feature_description} pairs; the model returns a score per feature and optionally a brief rationale. Features scoring ≥5\geq 5 are retained; the retained features’ activations are weighted by a sharpened cosine similarity between the feature text and the query (using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings) combined with the LLM score, capped at 50 features per query, and summed per user. This is the “weighted sum of activations on retained features” described in Section 5.

The weighted-sum combinator is itself compositional: each audience query is answered by combining contributions from multiple LLM-selected features rather than any single one, which is what allows the pipeline to cover both broad audiences (e.g., genre-level) and niche audiences (e.g., era ×\times sub-genre) without per-query structural changes.
